newsitem.title: USA: World Bank board approves reorganization plan.
newsitem.headline: World Bank board approves reorganization plan.

text.p: The World Bank executive board on Monday unanimously approved a $400 million plan to reorganize and reform the huge development institution, setting the stage for layoffs and a host of new products.

The plan, the brainchild of Bank President James Wolfensohn, was scaled back by $122 million from an earlier version when it came under fire from some countries, including the United States, for being too expensive at a time of tight budgets.
In its action, the Bank board also approved the first $60 million instalment to finance layoffs of some staff as the bank moves to cut overhead and spend more money in actual development activity.
The cost of the layoffs could amount to as much as $150 million, with perhaps 700 employees let go with severance packages, but the exact numbers are still uncertain.
The changes, called the strategic compact, will take place over the next 2-1/2 years, and are designed to make the bank more effective in achieving its basic mission of reducing poverty.
In a briefing for reporters, Wolfensohn emphasised that the Bank had to become more efficient and effective if it were to help reduce the growing gap between rich and poor in the world.
"The rich are getting richer and the poor are getting poorer," he said. "The lowest 20 percent of the world's population has 1.4 percent of the income and it's dropping."

Wolfensohn said that a goal of the reform package was to improve the effectiveness of the projects it supports. At present, some 34 percent of the projects get unsatisfactory ratings, and he will seek to cut that to 25 percent in the period ahead.

The bank is also exploring a number of new products that will make it easier for countries to achieve their goals of reducing poverty such as speeding up loans or allowing a quick rollover when projects are doing well and need more support.
As it has in the past, Wolfensohn said the Bank will continue to push countries to reduce corruption since this drains economic efficiency and turns off outside investment.
